claims.text: The multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy contains compositionally contrasting phases or constituents capable of forming protective oxides during thermal exposure.
Protective oxides such as Fe2O3, Cr2O3, or Al2O3 normally develop during elevated-temperature corrosion.
Simultaneous mechanical wear continuously disrupts or removes the nascent protective oxide films.
Removal of the protective film exposes vulnerable phase boundaries and microstructural heterogeneities.
Electrochemical-potential differences between dissimilar exposed phases create local galvanic cells.
Local galvanic coupling accelerates anodic dissolution of susceptible phases and localized corrosion.
The quality and integrity of the passive film control the alloy's corrosion resistance.
High-temperature exposure around 800 °C can accelerate corrosion in a chloride-containing environment.
Localized corrosion undermines the mechanical integrity of the worn surface and thereby further increases wear.
Mutual reinforcement between oxide removal, localized corrosion, and wear creates a positive feedback loop.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion produce a greater total degradation rate than matched wear-only or corrosion-only exposure.
The wear rate increases under coupled exposure because protective surface films are lost.
The corrosion response changes from relatively uniform passivation to localized pitting at phase boundaries under coupled exposure.
Coupled exposure increases both the depth and area of material loss relative to separate wear and corrosion tests.
The proposed mechanism applies near 800 °C in a NaCl environment when oxide formation and mechanical oxide removal occur concurrently.
The mechanism may cease to apply at substantially lower temperature or mechanical load.
A more adherent and wear-resistant pre-formed oxide should mitigate the coupled degradation.
Failure of pre-oxidation to significantly reduce combined degradation would falsify oxide-film removal as the primary cause of the acceleration.
